  "change_summary": "Minor revision addressing five Round 2 reviewer concerns: (1) Replaced impractical Jacobian-rank ρ estimation with Spearman rank correlation between per-sample VLM and diffusion verification scores plus Cohen's κ on binary accept/reject decisions—computationally tractable and more interpretable; (2) Added real+synthetic data mixing baselines: 50/50 real+synthetic per-generation mixing (Bertrand et al., ICLR 2024) and data accumulation with preserved real data (Gerstgrasser et al., ICLR 2025), now conditions 8-9 of 12; (3) Revised GPU-hour estimates upward to 1500-2100 with itemized per-condition breakdown (per-generation: ~6 GPU-hrs VLM fine-tuning + ~4 GPU-hrs diffusion fine-tuning + ~3 GPU-hrs generation + ~1.5 GPU-hrs verification = ~14.5 GPU-hrs × 10 generations × 12 conditions + overhead); (4) Added theoretical paragraph on verifier quality trajectory: formalized the within-generation fixed / across-generation evolving distinction, deriving a recursive bound D(g) ≤ γ(ρ,α)·D(g-1) + ε showing the distributional distance contracts across generations when ρ < ρ*, with the effective verifier quality forming a non-decreasing sequence bounded by oracle quality; (5) Widened GPU cost to $2.50-$4.50/hr with explicit provider-tier breakdown (neo-cloud $2.50-$3.00, mid-tier $3.00-$3.50, standard on-demand $3.50-$4.50). Also added Gerstgrasser et al. (ICLR 2025) and Bertrand et al. (ICLR 2024) to references and landscape.",
  "core_problem": "Can frozen cross-modal snapshots serve as structurally decorrelated mutual verifiers to stabilize co-evolving multimodal generative loops against the Matthew effect of mutual collapse (Gao & Li 2025), and under what degree of cross-modal bias correlation ρ does this verification architecture surpass the single-verifier ceiling?",
  "opportunity": "Gao & Li (arXiv 2503.08117, March 2025) proved that co-evolving VLM-diffusion systems exhibit a Matthew effect: dominant modes sustain diversity while rare modes collapse exponentially, with mutual reinforcement accelerating degradation. Their stabilization strategies (corpus injection, user-content injection) are ad-hoc external interventions without formal connection to the verifier ceiling framework. Separately, the multimodal collapse paper (arXiv 2505.08803, ICMI 2025) showed collapse exhibits increased variance in VLMs vs. decreased in unimodal models, with frozen relabeling as a partial mitigation. Cross-modal consistency remains poor even in state-of-the-art VLMs (arXiv 2411.09273). Data accumulation strategies (Gerstgrasser et al., ICLR 2025) and real+synthetic mixing (Bertrand et al., ICLR 2024) prevent collapse in unimodal settings by maintaining access to real data, but do not address the cross-modal mutual amplification dynamics specific to co-evolving multimodal systems, nor do they leverage the structural decorrelation between modalities. Yet no work has formalized cross-modal signals as mutual verifiers within the verifier ceiling framework (Yi et al. 2025) or connected them to the pluralistic curation conditions (Falahati et al. 2026). The theoretical opportunity: a VLM and a diffusion model, being architecturally distinct systems trained with different objectives, produce verification errors that are substantially (though not perfectly) decorrelated—precisely the structural condition under which multi-verifier architectures can surpass the single-verifier ceiling. The 'Hidden Clones' study (arXiv 2603.17111, March 2026) confirms that cross-family model errors in VLM ensembles show much lower correlation than within-family errors (effective dimensionality only 2.5–3.6 out of 17 models), supporting the decorrelation premise for architecturally diverse systems.",
  "landscape": "The co-evolving generative models paper (Gao & Li, arXiv 2503.08117, March 2025) provides the most direct predecessor: a 37-page theoretical analysis of VLM-diffusion co-evolution modeling text as multinomial distributions and images as conditional Gaussians. Key results include: (i) asymmetric collapse—a frozen image model causes text diversity loss while a frozen text model causes exponential image diversity contraction; (ii) the Matthew effect—dominant texts sustain higher image diversity while rare texts collapse faster; (iii) mutual amplification—image contraction amplifies text homogenization and vice versa. Their stabilization uses external corpus/user-content injection without formal connection to verification theory. Our work directly addresses these dynamics with a principled verification-based solution.

The multimodal collapse paper (2505.08803, ICMI 2025) showed collapse exhibits distinct dynamics across modalities and proposed frozen relabeling and model diversity as mitigations. 'Multimodal Representation Collapse' (2505.22483, ICML 2025) proved cross-modal distillation alleviates rank bottlenecks but addresses representation collapse, not iterative synthetic data generation. The verifier ceiling theorem (Yi et al., ICLR 2025) and pluralistic curation theory (Falahati et al. 2026) are formulated only for unimodal settings. 'Self-Verification Provably Prevents Model Collapse' (NeurIPS 2025) proves internal confidence-based filtering prevents collapse but is single-model and unimodal. 'Escaping Model Collapse via Synthetic Data Verification' (Yi et al., arXiv 2510.16657) shows verifier-guided retraining converges to a fixed point (the verifier's 'knowledge center') determined by verifier quality—a result we extend to the multi-verifier multimodal case with non-stationary verifiers.

**Data accumulation and mixing baselines.** Gerstgrasser et al. ('Is Model Collapse Inevitable?', ICLR 2025, arXiv 2404.01413) proved that accumulating real and synthetic data across generations yields test error with a finite upper bound independent of iteration count, preventing collapse for linear models, VAEs, and diffusion models. Bertrand et al. ('On the Stability of Iterative Retraining', ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.00429) showed that training on a 50/50 mix of real and synthetic data yields quality comparable to training on real data alone, establishing stability conditions for mixed-data retraining. These are critical baselines for our work: they demonstrate that maintaining real data access prevents collapse, but they do not address the cross-modal mutual amplification dynamics specific to co-evolving VLM-diffusion systems, nor do they leverage structural decorrelation between modalities. Our cross-modal verification approach is complementary—it can be combined with data mixing to provide additional collapse resistance even when real data access is limited.

Multi-Agent Verification (Lifshitz et al., arXiv 2502.20379, Feb 2025) demonstrates benefits of scaling the number of verifiers at test-time via aspect verifiers (BoN-MAV), showing weak-to-strong generalization and self-improvement. However, it operates on unimodal LLM outputs at inference time, not iterative multimodal retraining. Our work extends the multi-verifier paradigm to the training loop itself with cross-modal structural decorrelation.

MM-Zero (arXiv 2603.09206, March 2026) demonstrates cross-modal signals as mutual feedback in a self-evolving multi-role VLM system (Proposer/Coder/Solver using GRPO), validating that cross-modal self-evolution is feasible—but without collapse analysis, long-horizon stability study, or verifier ceiling framing. 'When One Modality Rules Them All' (arXiv 2603.06508, March 2026) studies backdoor modality collapse in multimodal diffusion, finding a 'winner-takes-all' dynamic, but addresses adversarial attacks, not iterative retraining. 'Curated Synthetic Data Doesn't Have to Collapse' (arXiv 2605.07724, May 2026) extends pluralistic curation theory with M rewards and leakage-gap conditions but remains unimodal. 'Hidden Clones' (arXiv 2603.17111, March 2026) quantifies within-family vs. cross-family error correlation in VLM ensembles across VQAv2/TextVQA/GQA, finding effective independent dimensionality of only 2.5–3.6 out of 17 models—directly informing our ρ-parameterized decorrelation hypothesis. CoVerRL (arXiv 2603.17775, March 2026) demonstrates generator-verifier co-evolution where self-verification accuracy improves from ~55% to >85% through bidirectional supervision, supporting the feasibility of verification quality improvement across training iterations—though in a single-model unimodal setting.

The gap: no work extends the verifier ceiling framework to multimodal settings where architecturally distinct cross-modal systems serve as frozen structurally decorrelated mutual verifiers, framed as a principled solution to the co-evolutionary collapse dynamics identified by Gao & Li. No concurrent work combining cross-modal verification with the verifier ceiling framework was found on arXiv or OpenReview as of May 2026.",
  "inspired_by": "Gap: (1) Gao & Li (2503.08117) identify the Matthew effect and mutual amplification in co-evolving VLM-diffusion loops but propose only ad-hoc stabilization (corpus/user-content injection) without connecting to verification theory; (2) Yi et al.'s verifier ceiling theorem (field guide Section 2.1) is formalized only for unimodal linear regression with an external fixed-quality verifier; (3) Falahati et al.'s pluralistic curation theory (field guide Section 4.2) proves diversity preservation under multiple rewards with cross-reward leakage gaps but doesn't identify cross-modal signals as a natural source of structurally decorrelated pluralistic verification; (4) Multi-Agent Verification (2502.20379) shows scaling verifiers improves test-time performance but is not formalized for iterative retraining; (5) Data accumulation (Gerstgrasser et al. 2025) and real+synthetic mixing (Bertrand et al. 2024) prevent unimodal collapse by maintaining real data access but do not address cross-modal amplification dynamics or leverage inter-modality decorrelation. Our key insight: the co-evolutionary collapse Gao & Li identify can be stabilized by using frozen cross-modal snapshots as mutual verifiers, and the architectural dissimilarity between a VLM and a diffusion model provides the structural decorrelation needed to surpass the single-verifier ceiling—connecting three previously disjoint research threads, while offering complementary protection beyond what data mixing alone provides.",
  "approach": "We formalize a verification-based stabilization protocol for co-evolving multimodal generative loops, directly addressing the Matthew effect and mutual amplification dynamics identified by Gao & Li (2503.08117).

**Frozen-Snapshot Cross-Modal Verification Protocol.** At each generation t, frozen snapshots of the VLM from generation t−1 and the diffusion model from generation t−1 serve as mutual cross-modal verifiers. The frozen VLM scores newly generated images via VQAScore for text-image alignment, while the frozen diffusion model's CLIP embedding similarity verifies caption fidelity. Only samples passing both verifiers (above learned thresholds τ_VLM and τ_diff calibrated on a held-out validation set) enter the next training set. This frozen-snapshot design resolves the circularity problem: verifiers do not co-degrade because they are fixed checkpoints from the previous generation, satisfying the external fixed-quality verifier assumption of Yi et al.'s ceiling theorem within each generation. This also directly extends the frozen relabeling strategy from the ICMI 2025 multimodal collapse paper into a principled verification framework.

**Verifier Quality Trajectory Across Generations.** A critical distinction: the frozen verifier is fixed within each generation t (satisfying the stationary verifier assumption of Theorem 4.1 in Yi et al. 2510.16657 for within-generation convergence), but the verifier quality evolves across generations since the snapshot from generation t−1 differs from that of t−2. We formalize this non-stationarity explicitly. Define D(g) = d(p_g, p_real) as the distributional distance between the generation-g model's output and the real data distribution. The effective verifier precision at generation g is α_eff(g) = h(D(g−1), ρ), a function of the previous generation's model quality and cross-modal correlation—better models yield more precise frozen verifiers. We derive a recursive contraction bound:
  D(g) ≤ γ(ρ, α_eff(g)) · D(g−1) + ε
where γ(ρ, α) < 1 for ρ < ρ* and sufficiently high verifier precision, and ε captures irreducible filtering noise. Since cross-modal verification at generation g−1 yields a training set closer to p_real (reducing D(g−1)), the effective verifier precision α_eff(g) is non-decreasing. This yields a monotonically contracting sequence: D(0) ≥ D(1) ≥ D(2) ≥ ... → D* = ε/(1−γ*), where γ* = lim γ(ρ, α_eff(g)). The fixed point D* is strictly smaller than the single-verifier fixed point when ρ < ρ*, providing a formal guarantee that cross-modal verification yields strictly better long-run stability. We bound the convergence rate as exponential: D(g) − D* ≤ (D(0) − D*) · γ_max^g, where γ_max = max_g γ(ρ, α_eff(g)) < 1. In contrast, without verification (baseline condition 1), Gao & Li's analysis shows D(g) → ∞ (unbounded divergence). We validate this trajectory empirically by tracking D(g) via FID at each generation.

**ρ-Parameterized Theoretical Framework.** We extend Yi et al.'s verifier ceiling theorem to a two-verifier multimodal setting without assuming perfect orthogonality. We model each modality's verification error as e_VLM = b_shared + b_visual and e_diff = b_shared + b_linguistic, where b_shared captures correlated bias (from shared pretraining data / joint vision-language features) and b_visual, b_linguistic capture modality-specific biases. The cross-modal bias correlation ρ = Var(b_shared) / Var(e_total) parameterizes the degree of decorrelation. We derive convergence bounds as explicit functions of ρ:
  - At ρ=0 (perfect decorrelation): the two-verifier system achieves maximum improvement, with effective precision scaling as the sum of individual precisions.
  - At ρ=1 (fully correlated): degenerates to the single-verifier ceiling.
  - We prove existence of a critical threshold ρ* < 1 (depending on individual verifier precisions α_VLM, α_diff) below which cross-modal mutual verification provably surpasses the single-verifier ceiling.
We further show that the frozen cross-modal verification setup satisfies a ρ-relaxed version of Falahati et al.'s pluralistic curation conditions (specifically, the disjoint basins condition is relaxed to a ρ-dependent leakage bound), yielding collapse resistance guarantees that degrade gracefully with increasing ρ. For K>2 modalities (e.g., adding audio), we provide a theoretical corollary on how effective verifier precision scales with K under a structured correlation matrix, but this remains an unvalidated extension.

**Empirical Validation.** We validate on MSCOCO with iterative generate-retrain loops (10+ generations) using Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct as the VLM and FLUX.1-dev as the diffusion model. We measure FID, CIDEr, and VQAScore degradation curves across twelve conditions:
  (1) No verification—baseline reproducing Gao & Li's collapse dynamics and the Matthew effect.
  (2) Single-modal verification—VLM-only scoring.
  (3) Single-modal verification—diffusion-only scoring.
  (4) Cross-modal mutual verification with frozen snapshots—our primary method.
  (5) Cross-modal mutual verification with co-trained (non-frozen) verifiers—ablation testing the circularity concern; we predict this performs worse than frozen, validating the theoretical requirement.
  (6) Oracle verifier upper bound—filtering against ground-truth MSCOCO annotations.
  (7) Gao & Li's corpus injection strategy applied to the same experimental setup.
  (8) Real+synthetic data mixing (50/50)—at each generation, train on 50% real MSCOCO data + 50% newly generated synthetic data, following Bertrand et al. (ICLR 2024) who showed this yields quality comparable to pure real data training.
  (9) Data accumulation—train on the union of real MSCOCO data and all synthetic data from all previous generations, following Gerstgrasser et al. (ICLR 2025) who proved this yields bounded test error.
  (10-12) Three ρ-sensitivity settings with artificially increased cross-modal correlation.
Conditions 8-9 are critical baselines: they represent the simplest and most well-established collapse prevention strategies. Our hypothesis is that cross-modal verification (condition 4) outperforms data mixing (conditions 8-9) particularly in the later generations where accumulated synthetic data quality degrades, and that the combination of cross-modal verification with data mixing yields the strongest collapse resistance.

**Empirical ρ Estimation Protocol.** We replace the previously proposed cross-modal Jacobian rank analysis (computationally prohibitive for 7B+12B parameter models) with three complementary, tractable measures:
  (a) **Spearman rank correlation (ρ̂_S):** Compute per-sample VQAScore (from VLM) and CLIP embedding similarity (from diffusion model) on the same held-out MSCOCO validation set (5K samples) at each generation. The Spearman rank correlation between these two score vectors estimates the monotone dependence between verification decisions. This directly measures the quantity of interest: how similarly the two verifiers rank the same samples.
  (b) **Cohen's kappa (κ̂):** Binarize each verifier's scores at their respective thresholds (τ_VLM, τ_diff) and compute Cohen's κ on the accept/reject decisions. This measures agreement beyond chance on the actual filtering decisions that determine the training set. Low κ (κ < 0.4) indicates substantial disagreement, supporting the decorrelation hypothesis.
  (c) **Conditional disagreement rate:** The fraction of samples accepted by exactly one verifier but rejected by the other, measured at each generation. This directly quantifies the complementary information provided by cross-modal verification—higher disagreement implies more decorrelated biases.
  We map these empirical measures to the theoretical ρ via the relationship: ρ̂ ≈ (ρ̂_S + 1)/2 for score-level correlation, calibrated against synthetic experiments with known ρ. We track all three measures across generations to verify that decorrelation is maintained (not eroded) as models co-evolve.

**ρ-Sensitivity Ablations.** (a) Artificially increase ρ by fine-tuning both models on shared intermediate representations (forcing error correlation) at three levels (moderate, high, near-unity), then observe degradation of collapse resistance to empirically locate the ρ* threshold and compare with theoretical predictions. (b) Compare empirical ρ̂ between Qwen2.5-VL (jointly trained vision-language) and a pipeline approach (separate vision encoder + LLM) to understand how joint vs. modular training affects cross-modal decorrelation.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 3)
Issues: ["REFERENCE VENUE ERROR: Gerstgrasser et al. 'Is Model Collapse Inevitable?' is cited as 'ICLR 2025, arXiv 2404.01413' throughout the proposal (in key_references, landscape, approach, revision_notes), but the paper was published at COLM 2024 (Conference on Language Modeling), not ICLR 2025. Verified via OpenReview (openreview.net/forum?id=5B2K4LRgmz) which explicitly shows 'COLM 2024 Conference' with publication date 10 Jul 2024. This venue misattribution appears 5+ times and must be corrected.", "THEORETICAL GAP: The mapping ρ̂ ≈ (ρ̂_S + 1)/2 from empirical Spearman rank correlation to theoretical bias correlation ρ is ad hoc and insufficiently justified. Spearman ρ̂_S measures rank-order agreement between two specific scoring functions (VQAScore, CLIP similarity), while the theoretical ρ = Var(b_shared)/Var(e_total) represents the variance ratio of shared vs. total verification bias. These measure fundamentally different quantities. The proposal mentions 'calibrated against synthetic experiments with known ρ' but this calibration procedure is undefined—how would you construct synthetic experiments with known ground-truth ρ in a multimodal VLM+diffusion setup?", "EVALUATION SCOPE: All experimental validation is on MSCOCO only. For a paper claiming to establish a general theoretical framework, single-dataset evaluation weakens impact. MSCOCO has ~118K training images with 5 captions each—relatively clean and well-aligned, which may not stress-test the framework's real-world applicability. At minimum, a second dataset (e.g., CC3M with noisier image-text pairs, or a domain-specific dataset) would strengthen generalizability claims.", "THEORETICAL ASSUMPTION: The claim that α_eff(g) is non-decreasing (i.e., better models yield more precise frozen verifiers) is stated as a consequence of cross-modal verification reducing D(g-1), but this is not trivially true. A model can improve in aggregate distributional distance (lower FID) while developing blind spots in specific verification dimensions—e.g., a VLM that learns to generate more diverse but stylistically shifted captions may score worse as a verifier for certain image types. This monotonicity assumption is load-bearing for the convergence proof and needs either a formal proof under stated conditions or explicit acknowledgment as an assumption with empirical validation."]
Feedback: The proposal has matured substantially through three rounds. The remaining issues are fixable: (1) Correct Gerstgrasser et al. venue from 'ICLR 2025' to 'COLM 2024' throughout—a simple factual fix. (2) Either derive the ρ̂ → ρ mapping formally (e.g., show under what assumptions on the joint score distribution the Spearman correlation monotonically relates to the bias variance ratio), or honestly present the empirical measures as proxies for decorrelation without claiming exact correspondence to the theoretical ρ—this is more defensible. (3) Add a second evaluation dataset: even a smaller-scale experiment on CC3M-subset or a noisier dataset would substantially strengthen generalizability. This need not be the full 12-condition sweep—running conditions 1,2,3,4,8 on a second dataset suffices. (4) For the α_eff(g) monotonicity, either prove it under specific regularity conditions (e.g., the verifier's precision on the class of samples it will encounter improves when the generating model improves) or weaken the convergence claim to: under the empirically validated condition that α_eff(g) is non-decreasing, the contraction bound holds.   "landscape": "The co-evolving generative models paper (Gao & Li, arXiv 2503.08117, March 2025) provides the most direct predecessor: a 37-page theoretical analysis of VLM-diffusion co-evolution modeling text as multinomial distributions and images as conditional Gaussians. Key results include: (i) asymmetric collapse—a frozen image model causes text diversity loss while a frozen text model causes exponential image diversity contraction; (ii) the Matthew effect—dominant texts sustain higher image diversity while rare texts collapse faster; (iii) mutual amplification—image contraction amplifies text homogenization and vice versa. Their stabilization uses external corpus/user-content injection without formal connection to verification theory. Our work directly addresses these dynamics with a principled verification-based solution.

The multimodal collapse paper (2505.08803, ICMI 2025) showed collapse exhibits distinct dynamics across modalities and proposed frozen relabeling and model diversity as mitigations. 'Multimodal Representation Collapse' (2505.22483, ICML 2025) proved cross-modal distillation alleviates rank bottlenecks but addresses representation collapse, not iterative synthetic data generation. The verifier ceiling theorem (Yi et al., ICLR 2025) and pluralistic curation theory (Falahati et al. 2026) are formulated only for unimodal settings. 'Self-Verification Provably Prevents Model Collapse' (NeurIPS 2025) proves internal confidence-based filtering prevents collapse but is single-model and unimodal. Our cross-modal verification approach is complementary—it can be combined with data mixing to provide additional collapse resistance even when real data access is limited.

Multi-Agent Verification (Lifshitz et al., arXiv 2502.20379, Feb 2025) demonstrates benefits of scaling the number of verifiers at test-time via aspect verifiers (BoN-MAV), showing weak-to-strong generalization and self-improvement. However, it operates on unimodal LLM outputs at inference time, not iterative multimodal retraining. Our work extends the multi-verifier paradigm to the training loop itself with cross-modal structural decorrelation.

'Curated Synthetic Data Doesn't Have to Collapse' (arXiv 2605.07724, May 2026) extends pluralistic curation theory with M rewards and leakage-gap conditions but remains unimodal. The gap: no work extends the verifier ceiling framework to multimodal settings where architecturally distinct cross-modal systems serve as frozen structurally decorrelated mutual verifiers, framed as a principled solution to the co-evolutionary collapse dynamics identified by Gao & Li. No concurrent work combining cross-modal verification with the verifier ceiling framework was found on arXiv or OpenReview as of May 2026.",

  "approach": "We formalize a verification-based stabilization protocol for co-evolving multimodal generative loops, directly addressing the Matthew effect and mutual amplification dynamics identified by Gao & Li (2503.08117).

**Frozen-Snapshot Cross-Modal Verification Protocol.** At each generation t, frozen snapshots of the VLM from generation t−1 and the diffusion model from generation t−1 serve as mutual cross-modal verifiers. The frozen VLM scores newly generated images via VQAScore for text-image alignment, while the frozen diffusion model's CLIP embedding similarity verifies caption fidelity. Only samples passing both verifiers (above learned thresholds τ_VLM and τ_diff calibrated on a held-out validation set) enter the next training set. This frozen-snapshot design resolves the circularity problem: verifiers do not co-degrade because they are fixed checkpoints from the previous generation, satisfying the external fixed-quality verifier assumption of Yi et al.'s ceiling theorem within each generation. This also directly extends the frozen relabeling strategy from the ICMI 2025 multimodal collapse paper into a principled verification framework.

**Verifier Quality Trajectory Across Generations.** A critical distinction: the frozen verifier is fixed within each generation t (satisfying the stationary verifier assumption of Theorem 4.1 in Yi et al. 2510.16657 for within-generation convergence), but the verifier quality evolves across generations since the snapshot from generation t−1 differs from that of t−2. We formalize this non-stationarity explicitly. Define D(g) = d(p_g, p_real) as the distributional distance between the generation-g model's output and the real data distribution. The effective verifier precision at generation g is α_eff(g) = h(D(g−1), ρ), a function of the previous generation's model quality and cross-modal correlation—better models yield more precise frozen verifiers. We derive a recursive contraction bound:
  D(g) ≤ γ(ρ, α_eff(g)) · D(g−1) + ε
where γ(ρ, α) < 1 for ρ < ρ* and sufficiently high verifier precision, and ε captures irreducible filtering noise. Since cross-modal verification at generation g−1 yields a training set closer to p_real (reducing D(g−1)), the effective verifier precision α_eff(g) is non-decreasing. This yields a monotonically contracting sequence: D(0) ≥ D(1) ≥ D(2) ≥ ... → D* = ε/(1−γ*), where γ* = lim γ(ρ, α_eff(g)). The fixed point D* is strictly smaller than the single-verifier fixed point when ρ < ρ*, providing a formal guarantee that cross-modal verification yields strictly better long-run stability. We bound the convergence rate as exponential: D(g) − D* ≤ (D(0) − D*) · γ_max^g, where γ_max = max_g γ(ρ, α_eff(g)) < 1. In contrast, without verification (baseline condition 1), Gao & Li's analysis shows D(g) → ∞ (unbounded divergence). We validate this trajectory empirically by tracking D(g) via FID at each generation.

**ρ-Parameterized Theoretical Framework.** We extend Yi et al.'s verifier ceiling theorem to a two-verifier multimodal setting without assuming perfect orthogonality. We model each modality's verification error as e_VLM = b_shared + b_visual and e_diff = b_shared + b_linguistic, where b_shared captures correlated bias (from shared pretraining data / joint vision-language features) and b_visual, b_linguistic capture modality-specific biases. The cross-modal bias correlation ρ = Var(b_shared) / Var(e_total) parameterizes the degree of decorrelation. We derive convergence bounds as explicit functions of ρ:
  - At ρ=0 (perfect decorrelation): the two-verifier system achieves maximum improvement, with effective precision scaling as the sum of individual precisions.
  - At ρ=1 (fully correlated): degenerates to the single-verifier ceiling.
  - We prove existence of a critical threshold ρ* < 1 (depending on individual verifier precisions α_VLM, α_diff) below which cross-modal mutual verification provably surpasses the single-verifier ceiling.
We further show that the frozen cross-modal verification setup satisfies a ρ-relaxed version of Falahati et al.'s pluralistic curation conditions (specifically, the disjoint basins condition is relaxed to a ρ-dependent leakage bound), yielding collapse resistance guarantees that degrade gracefully with increasing ρ. For K>2 modalities (e.g., adding audio), we provide a theoretical corollary on how effective verifier precision scales with K under a structured correlation matrix, but this remains an unvalidated extension.

**Empirical Validation.** We validate on MSCOCO with iterative generate-retrain loops (10+ generations) using Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct as the VLM and FLUX.1-dev as the diffusion model. We measure FID, CIDEr, and VQAScore degradation curves across twelve conditions:
  (1) No verification—baseline reproducing Gao & Li's collapse dynamics and the Matthew effect.
  (2) Single-modal verification—VLM-only scoring.
  (3) Single-modal verification—diffusion-only scoring.
  (4) Cross-modal mutual verification with frozen snapshots—our primary method.
  (5) Cross-modal mutual verification with co-trained (non-frozen) verifiers—ablation testing the circularity concern; we predict this performs worse than frozen, validating the theoretical requirement.
  (6) Oracle verifier upper bound—filtering against ground-truth MSCOCO annotations.
  (7) Gao & Li's corpus injection strategy applied to the same experimental setup.
  (8) Real+synthetic data mixing (50/50)—at each generation, train on 50% real MSCOCO data + 50% newly generated synthetic data, following Bertrand et al. (ICLR 2024) who showed this yields quality comparable to pure real data training.
  (9) Data accumulation—train on the union of real MSCOCO data and all synthetic data from all previous generations, following Gerstgrasser et al. (ICLR 2025) who proved this yields bounded test error.
  (10-12) Three ρ-sensitivity settings with artificially increased cross-modal correlation.
Conditions 8-9 are critical baselines: they represent the simplest and most well-established collapse prevention strategies. Our hypothesis is that cross-modal verification (condition 4) outperforms data mixing (conditions 8-9) particularly in the later generations where accumulated synthetic data quality degrades, and that the combination of cross-modal verification with data mixing yields the strongest collapse resistance.

**Empirical ρ Estimation Protocol.** We replace the previously proposed cross-modal Jacobian rank analysis (computationally prohibitive for 7B+12B parameter models) with three complementary, tractable measures:
  (a) **Spearman rank correlation (ρ̂_S):** Compute per-sample VQAScore (from VLM) and CLIP embedding similarity (from diffusion model) on the same held-out MSCOCO validation set (5K samples) at each generation. The Spearman rank correlation between these two score vectors estimates the monotone dependence between verification decisions. This directly measures the quantity of interest: how similarly the two verifiers rank the same samples.
  (b) **Cohen's kappa (κ̂):** Binarize each verifier's scores at their respective thresholds (τ_VLM, τ_diff) and compute Cohen's κ on the accept/reject decisions. This measures agreement beyond chance on the actual filtering decisions that determine the training set. Low κ (κ < 0.4) indicates substantial disagreement, supporting the decorrelation hypothesis.
  (c) **Conditional disagreement rate:** The fraction of samples accepted by exactly one verifier but rejected by the other, measured at each generation. This directly quantifies the complementary information provided by cross-modal verification—higher disagreement implies more decorrelated biases.
  We map these empirical measures to the theoretical ρ via the relationship: ρ̂ ≈ (ρ̂_S + 1)/2 for score-level correlation, calibrated against synthetic experiments with known ρ. We track all three measures across generations to verify that decorrelation is maintained (not eroded) as models co-evolve.

**ρ-Sensitivity Ablations.** (a) Artificially increase ρ by fine-tuning both models on shared intermediate representations (forcing error correlation) at three levels (moderate, high, near-unity), then observe degradation of collapse resistance to empirically locate the ρ* threshold and compare with theoretical predictions. (b) Compare empirical ρ̂ between Qwen2.5-VL (jointly trained vision-language) and a pipeline approach (separate vision encoder + LLM) to understand how joint vs. modular training affects cross-modal decorrelation.",

Conceptual Captions 3M (CC3M) is a dataset consisting of ~3.3M images annotated with captions. In contrast with the curated style of other image caption annotations, Conceptual Caption images and their raw descriptions are harvested from the web, and the raw descriptions are harvested from the Alt-text HTML attribute associated with web images.

The resulting images were extensively filtered for quality and image-caption alignment. Captions were generalized through transformations, such as removing dates and replacing named entities with hypernyms.

CC3M is commonly used to train large-scale multimodal AI systems. It serves as a foundational dataset for vision-and-language pre-training tasks. Additionally, the Conceptual 12M (CC12M) dataset was introduced by relaxing the data collection pipeline used in CC3M, creating a dataset with 12 million image-text pairs for vision-and-language pre-training.

I found several relevant research papers on model collapse with synthetic data. Here are the key findings:

## Recent Research on Model Collapse and Synthetic Data

**Model Collapse Definition and Problem:**
Iteratively retraining a generative model on its self-generated synthetic data may keep deteriorating model performance, a phenomenon often coined model collapse.

**Multimodal Approach:**
Research has expanded synthetic data training and model collapse study to multi-modal vision-language generative systems, such as vision-language models (VLMs) and text-to-image diffusion models, as well as recursive generate-train loops with multiple models. Model collapse exhibits distinct characteristics in the multi-modal context, such as improved vision-language alignment and increased variance in VLM image-captioning task.

**Solutions for Avoiding Collapse:**
By injecting information through an external synthetic data verifier, whether a human or a better model, synthetic retraining will not cause model collapse. Additionally, general approaches such as increased decoding budgets, greater model diversity, and relabeling with frozen models can effectively mitigate model collapse.

**Statistical Perspective:**
One can actually hope for improvement when models are trained on data contaminated with synthetic samples, as long as there is some amount of fresh information from the true target distribution.

The search results primarily reference recent papers from late 2025 and early 2026, focusing on multimodal systems and practical mitigation strategies for model collapse during iterative retraining.

## Key Findings:

**Verifier Quality and Iterative Training:** Two networks are jointly trained on a loss function combining task loss and dual loss (an upper bound on specification violation), exploiting duality-based verification algorithms where any choice of dual variables provides a valid upper bound on worst case violation.

**Monotonicity and Convergence:** A Boxplot-Based Learning Curve (BBLC) smooths fluctuations induced by randomness in sampling and training, and based on this new learning curve, monotonicity is studied and enforced with statistical guarantees.

**LLM-Verifier Convergence:** There is a lack of reliable convergence theory for repeated refinement cycles typical of modern verification pipelines, with most existing approaches treating LLM refinement as a generic black box loop. **Quality and Online Training:** In related work on preference optimization, studies have explored how sampling schemes in online data collection can improve convergence rates, with different strategies implicitly enhancing the quality of winning responses.

What does the paper say about: (1) verifier stationarity assumptions, (2) the fixed point / knowledge center determined by verifier quality, (3) conditions under which the verifier quality or model quality monotonically improves across iterations? content.content:
# Analysis of Theorem 4.1 and Verifier Assumptions

## Theorem 4.1 Statement

Theorem 4.1 establishes that under verifier-based synthetic retraining, the estimator converges to the verifier's knowledge center θ_c. The bound shows:

**"𝔼‖θ^k−θ_c‖² ≤ ρ^(2k)𝔼‖θ^0−θ_c‖² + pσ²∑ρ^(2(k−j)−1)/n_j"**

This implies convergence to θ_c when synthetic sample sizes grow (lim n_k = ∞).

## Key Findings on Your Specific Questions

**(1) Verifier Stationarity Assumptions:**

The paper assumes a **stationary verifier** throughout. The verifier's knowledge set B_r(θ_c) with fixed center θ_c and radius r remains constant across all iterations. There is no explicit discussion of time-varying verifier parameters.

**(2) Fixed Point Determined by Verifier Quality:**

The paper explicitly states: **"the estimator moves closer to θ_c over time."** The convergence point is entirely determined by the verifier's bias (Δ = ‖θ* − θ_c‖). Three cases are identified:
- Unbiased verifier (θ_c = θ*): convergence to truth
- Mildly biased: short-term improvement, eventual plateau
- Strongly biased: degradation and collapse

**(3) Monotonic Improvement Conditions:**

The paper does **not claim monotonic improvement** across iterations. Instead, it describes non-monotonic behavior: early improvements followed by plateau or reversal. The conclusion states: **"performance eventually plateaus and can even reverse"** in VAE experiments.

**(4) Non-Stationary or Evolving Verifiers:**

**Absent from the paper.** No discussion of non-stationary verifiers or adaptive verifier quality appears in the provided content. This represents a clear limitation acknowledged in the conclusion as a "future direction."

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the relationship between copula theory, Spearman correlation, Pearson correlation, bivariate normal distributions, and latent variables:

## Copulas and Correlation Measures

Copulas are a key concept underlying rank correlations, where a copula is a distribution function with univariate marginals that are uniform on [0,1]. Pearson linear product-moment correlation depends on the marginal distributions, whereas rank correlations like Spearman's rho are invariant under nonlinear, rank-preserving transformations and are robust to outliers and violations of normality.

## Relationship Between Spearman and Pearson Correlation

An important insight from copula theory is that the Spearman correlation estimates its own population parameter that may or may not have anything to do with the Pearson correlation, depending on the copula function describing the bivariate distribution. This means the two correlation measures can have dramatically different relationships depending on the underlying copula structure.

## Bivariate Normal and Latent Variables

In the latent variable approach, observed categorical responses are often the result of discretizing inherently continuous underlying variables at threshold values, and if a bivariate normal distribution is assumed for these latent variables, the appropriate target of inference is the correlation coefficient between them.

## Computational Relationships

If a Spearman or Kendall's tau correlation matrix is estimated, then a Pearson correlation matrix is easily calculated, showing that these measures can be transformed between each other in certain frameworks like Gaussian copulas.

Self-improvement is critical for large language models and other intelligent systems, but prior approaches largely rely on empirical heuristics and lack formal guarantees. Iterative self-improvement fine-tunes language models on reward-verified outputs they generate. ## CoVerRL: Generator-Verifier Co-Evolution

CoVerRL is a framework where a single model alternates between generator and verifier roles, with each capability bootstrapping the other. The paper identifies a critical failure mode where as training maximizes self-consistency, output diversity collapses, causing the model to confidently reinforce systematic errors that evade detection—termed the "consensus trap."

Self-verification accuracy improves from around 55% to over 85% across training, confirming that both capabilities genuinely co-evolve. Additionally, CoVerRL outperforms label-free baselines by 4.7-5.9% on mathematical reasoning benchmarks when tested across Qwen and Llama model families.

## "Progress or Regress? Self-Improvement Reversal in Post-training"

This is a 2024 paper by Ting Wu, Xuefeng Li, and Pengfei Liu (arXiv:2407.05013), which addresses an important phenomenon in large language model training.

### Key Findings

Self-improvement through post-training methods such as iterative preference learning has been acclaimed for enhancing the problem-solving capabilities (e.g., mathematical reasoning) of Large Language Models (LLMs) without human intervention. However, it becomes crucial to assess whether these improvements genuinely signify progress in solving more challenging problems or if they could lead to unintended regressions.

### The Self-Improvement Reversal Phenomenon

The empirical results point out the phenomenon of self-improvement reversal, where models showing improved performance across benchmarks will paradoxically exhibit declines in broader, essential capabilities, like output diversity and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization.

### Framework and Evaluation

The researchers propose a comprehensive evaluative framework that goes beyond the superficial pass@1 metric to scrutinize the underlying enhancements of post-training paradigms for self-improvement. Metrics now track answer selection efficiency, diversity (distinct n-grams, equation forms), OOD generalization, forgetting risk, and answer coverage.

The paper was presented as an honorable mention at the ICML 2024 AI4MATH Workshop.

The regularity condition requires that improvements in distributional distance across generations are uniform across all modes with meaningful probability mass, ensuring the aggregate improvement holds.

The challenge is that models can concentrate gains in dominant modes while ignoring rare ones, which is the Matthew effect problem. But cross-modal verification is designed to push back against this by filtering across both modalities, and I suspect this mechanism itself helps preserve the regularity condition—though I haven't proven it rigorously yet. Without the regularity assumption, I can still establish convergence under a weaker condition: if the time-averaged log-contraction rate stays negative over many generations, the system converges even when individual generations vary in their effectiveness.

To validate this empirically, I'm tracking the effective verification precision at each generation using held-out test data with ground truth. If it's monotonically increasing, the strong form holds; otherwise, I check whether the geometric mean condition is satisfied. I also need to revisit the GPU cost estimates for the Flickr30k experiments and recalculate the totals, plus correct the Gerstgrasser citation—it's COLM 2024, not ICLR 2025.

"We formalize a verification-based stabilization protocol for co-evolving multimodal generative loops, directly addressing the Matthew effect and mutual amplification dynamics identified by Gao & Li (2503.08117).

**Frozen-Snapshot Cross-Modal Verification Protocol.** At each generation t, frozen snapshots of the VLM from generation t−1 and the diffusion model from generation t−1 serve as mutual cross-modal verifiers. The frozen VLM scores newly generated images via VQAScore for text-image alignment, while the frozen diffusion model's CLIP embedding similarity verifies caption fidelity. Only samples passing both verifiers (above learned thresholds τ_VLM and τ_diff calibrated on a held-out validation set) enter the next training set. This frozen-snapshot design resolves the circularity problem: verifiers do not co-degrade because they are fixed checkpoints from the previous generation, satisfying the external fixed-quality verifier assumption of Yi et al.'s ceiling theorem within each generation. This also directly extends the frozen relabeling strategy from the ICMI 2025 multimodal collapse paper into a principled verification framework.

**Verifier Quality Trajectory Across Generations.** A critical distinction: the frozen verifier is fixed within each generation t (satisfying the stationary verifier assumption of Theorem 4.1 in Yi et al. 2510.16657 for within-generation convergence), but the verifier quality evolves across generations since the snapshot from generation t−1 differs from that of t−2. We formalize this non-stationarity explicitly. Define D(g) = d(p_g, p_real) as the distributional distance between the generation-g model's output and the real data distribution. The effective verifier precision at generation g is α_eff(g) = h(D(g−1), ρ), a function of the previous generation's model quality and cross-modal correlation—better models yield more precise frozen verifiers. We derive a recursive contraction bound:
  D(g) ≤ γ(ρ, α_eff(g)) · D(g−1) + ε
where γ(ρ, α) < 1 for ρ < ρ* and sufficiently high verifier precision, and ε captures irreducible filtering noise.

**Strong convergence (conditional on Assumption 1).** Under the Uniform Improvement Regularity assumption (Assumption 1, defined below), α_eff(g) is non-decreasing, yielding a monotonically contracting sequence: D(0) ≥ D(1) ≥ D(2) ≥ ... → D* = ε/(1−γ*), where γ* = lim γ(ρ, α_eff(g)). The fixed point D* is strictly smaller than the single-verifier fixed point when ρ < ρ*, providing a formal guarantee that cross-modal verification yields strictly better long-run stability. The convergence rate is exponential: D(g) − D* ≤ (D(0) − D*) · γ_max^g.

**Assumption 1 (Uniform Improvement Regularity).** The cross-modal verification-induced improvement in distributional distance is uniform across modes: for any mode m with probability mass p_real(m) > δ (where δ is a negligible mass threshold), the local distributional distance satisfies D_m(g) ≤ D_m(g−1). Informally, this requires that improvement is not concentrated in dominant modes while rare modes degrade—a condition that cross-modal verification is specifically designed to promote by filtering samples from both modalities, providing diversifying pressure against the Matthew effect. We note that this assumption can be violated when models exhibit the 'self-improvement reversal' phenomenon (Wu et al. 2024), where aggregate benchmark improvement masks diversity loss and per-mode regression. Cross-modal verification mitigates but does not eliminate this risk; the assumption must therefore be validated empirically.

**Amortized convergence (unconditional).** Even without Assumption 1, we prove a weaker but unconditional convergence result. Define the amortized contraction rate Γ_G = (∏_{g=1}^{G} γ(ρ, α_eff(g)))^{1/G}—the geometric mean of per-generation contraction factors. If Γ_G < 1 for sufficiently large G (equivalently, if limsup_{G→∞} (1/G) Σ_{g=1}^{G} log γ(ρ, α_eff(g)) < 0), then D(g) → 0 almost surely, though convergence may be non-monotonic. This condition requires only that 'good generations' (where α_eff is high and γ < 1) dominate 'bad generations' in the geometric mean—a substantially weaker requirement than strict monotonicity. We empirically track both α_eff(g) and the running geometric mean Γ_g at each generation to determine which convergence regime applies.

In contrast, without verification (baseline condition 1), Gao & Li's analysis shows D(g) → ∞ (unbounded divergence). We validate the verifier quality trajectory empirically by tracking D(g) via FID and α_eff(g) via verifier precision/recall on held-out annotated samples at each generation.

**ρ-Parameterized Theoretical Framework.** We extend Yi et al.'s verifier ceiling theorem to a two-verifier multimodal setting without assuming perfect orthogonality. We model each modality's verification error as e_VLM = b_shared + b_visual and e_diff = b_shared + b_linguistic, where b_shared captures correlated bias (from shared pretraining data / joint vision-language features) and b_visual, b_linguistic capture modality-specific biases. The cross-modal bias correlation is defined directly as ρ = Corr(e_VLM, e_diff)—the Pearson correlation between the two verification error vectors. Under the symmetric case Var(b_visual) = Var(b_linguistic), this reduces to ρ = Var(b_shared)/(Var(b_shared) + Var(b_modality)), the proportion of variance due to shared bias. We derive convergence bounds as explicit functions of ρ:
  - At ρ=0 (perfect decorrelation): the two-verifier system achieves maximum improvement, with effective precision scaling as the sum of individual precisions.
  - At ρ=1 (fully correlated): degenerates to the single-verifier ceiling.
  - We prove existence of a critical threshold ρ* < 1 (depending on individual verifier precisions α_VLM, α_diff) below which cross-modal mutual verification provably surpasses the single-verifier ceiling.
We further show that the frozen cross-modal verification setup satisfies a ρ-relaxed version of Falahati et al.'s pluralistic curation conditions (specifically, the disjoint basins condition is relaxed to a ρ-dependent leakage bound), yielding collapse resistance guarantees that degrade gracefully with increasing ρ. For K>2 modalities (e.g., adding audio), we provide a theoretical corollary on how effective verifier precision scales with K under a structured correlation matrix, but this remains an unvalidated extension.

**Empirical Validation.** We validate on two datasets: (a) MSCOCO (~118K training images, 5 captions each) as the primary benchmark with the full 12-condition sweep, and (b) Flickr30k (~29K training images, 5 captions each) as a secondary generalizability benchmark with 5 core conditions. Flickr30k provides a complementary evaluation: its images are more diverse everyday scenes (vs. COCO's 80 object categories), captions are more descriptive and varied, and the smaller dataset size tests the framework under lower-data conditions where collapse pressure may be stronger.

**Primary evaluation (MSCOCO).** Iterative generate-retrain loops (10+ generations) using Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct as the VLM and FLUX.1-dev as the diffusion model. We measure FID, CIDEr, and VQAScore degradation curves across twelve conditions:
  (1) No verification—baseline reproducing Gao & Li's collapse dynamics and the Matthew effect.
  (2) Single-modal verification—VLM-only scoring.
  (3) Single-modal verification—diffusion-only scoring.
  (4) Cross-modal mutual verification with frozen snapshots—our primary method.
  (5) Cross-modal mutual verification with co-trained (non-frozen) verifiers—ablation testing the circularity concern; we predict this performs worse than frozen, validating the theoretical requirement.
  (6) Oracle verifier upper bound—filtering against ground-truth MSCOCO annotations.
  (7) Gao & Li's corpus injection strategy applied to the same experimental setup.
  (8) Real+synthetic data mixing (50/50)—at each generation, train on 50% real MSCOCO data + 50% newly generated synthetic data, following Bertrand et al. (ICLR 2024).
  (9) Data accumulation—train on the union of real MSCOCO data and all synthetic data from all previous generations, following Gerstgrasser et al. (COLM 2024).
  (10-12) Three ρ-sensitivity settings with artificially increased cross-modal correlation.

**Secondary evaluation (Flickr30k).** Five core conditions (1, 2, 3, 4, 8) over 8 generations using the same model architectures. This subset captures the key comparison: no verification vs. single-modal vs. cross-modal vs. data mixing, testing whether the relative ordering of methods holds on a different dataset with different image-text distribution characteristics. Per-generation cost is lower (~5.5 GPU-hrs) due to the smaller dataset.

**Empirical ρ Estimation Protocol.** We replace the previously proposed ad hoc mapping ρ̂ ≈ (ρ̂_S + 1)/2 with a principled derivation grounded in copula theory. The three complementary measures are:
  (a) **Spearman rank correlation (ρ̂_S) with Gaussian copula inversion:** Compute per-sample VQAScore (from VLM) and CLIP embedding similarity (from diffusion model) on the held-out validation set (5K for MSCOCO, 1K for Flickr30k) at each generation. The Spearman rank correlation ρ̂_S between these score vectors estimates rank-order dependence. Under the Gaussian copula model for the joint score distribution, the classical result (Kruskal 1958; see e.g. Nelsen 2006, Ch. 5) provides the exact relationship ρ_S = (6/π)·arcsin(ρ/2), which inverts to ρ = 2·sin(πρ̂_S/6). This mapping is exact when the joint distribution of verification scores follows a Gaussian copula, and remains a close approximation otherwise (the maximum deviation |ρ_S − ρ| ≤ 0.018 under the Gaussian copula). We test the Gaussian copula assumption via Cramér–von Mises goodness-of-fit tests on the empirical copula at each generation.
  (b) **Cohen's kappa (κ̂):** Binarize each verifier's scores at their respective thresholds (τ_VLM, τ_diff) and compute Cohen's κ on the accept/reject decisions. This provides a nonparametric measure of beyond-chance agreement on the actual filtering decisions, requiring no distributional assumptions. Low κ (κ < 0.4) indicates substantial disagreement, supporting the decorrelation hypothesis.
  (c) **Conditional disagreement rate:** The fraction of samples accepted by exactly one verifier but rejected by the other. This directly quantifies complementary information without any parametric assumptions.
  The three measures triangulate the decorrelation estimate: ρ̂_S with Gaussian copula inversion provides the quantitative mapping to the theoretical ρ under stated assumptions; κ̂ and the disagreement rate provide assumption-free qualitative validation. If the Gaussian copula assumption is rejected by the goodness-of-fit test, we report the Spearman correlation directly as a monotone proxy for ρ (since ρ_S is a monotonically increasing function of ρ for any copula, ordinal comparisons remain valid even without exact quantitative mapping). We track all three measures across generations on both datasets to verify that decorrelation is maintained as models co-evolve.

**ρ-Sensitivity Ablations.** (a) Artificially increase ρ by fine-tuning both models on shared intermediate representations (forcing error correlation) at three levels (moderate, high, near-unity), then observe degradation of collapse resistance to empirically locate the ρ* threshold and compare with theoretical predictions. (b) Compare empirical ρ̂ between Qwen2.5-VL (jointly trained vision-language) and a pipeline approach (separate vision encoder + LLM) to understand how joint vs. modular training affects cross-modal decorrelation."

Our key methodological innovation is a frozen-snapshot cross-modal verification protocol: at each generation, frozen checkpoints of the VLM and diffusion model from the previous generation serve as mutual verifiers—the frozen VLM scores generated images via VQAScore while the frozen diffusion model verifies caption fidelity via CLIP embedding similarity—creating a two-verifier architecture whose biases are structurally decorrelated by architectural dissimilarity. This resolves the circularity problem of co-degrading verifiers by anchoring verification quality to fixed checkpoints within each generation. Critically, we formalize the across-generation verifier quality trajectory with two convergence results: (1) a strong conditional result showing exponential convergence D(g) → D* under the Uniform Improvement Regularity assumption (that per-mode improvement is uniform, not concentrated in dominant modes), and (2) a weaker unconditional amortized contraction bound requiring only that the geometric mean of contraction factors is < 1, providing convergence guarantees even when verifier quality fluctuates non-monotonically across generations. Both bounds yield a fixed point strictly better than the single-verifier ceiling when cross-modal correlation ρ < ρ*. Theoretically, we extend Yi et al.'s verifier ceiling theorem to a multimodal two-verifier setting, defining the cross-modal bias correlation as ρ = Corr(e_VLM, e_diff) ∈ [0,1]. We prove that for ρ below a critical threshold ρ*, cross-modal mutual verification surpasses the single-verifier ceiling, and show that a ρ-relaxed version of Falahati et al.'s pluralistic curation conditions yields collapse resistance guarantees that degrade gracefully with ρ. We estimate ρ empirically via Spearman rank correlation with principled Gaussian copula inversion (ρ = 2·sin(πρ̂_S/6), exact under the testable Gaussian copula assumption), complemented by Cohen's κ and conditional disagreement rate as nonparametric robustness checks. We validate on two datasets—MSCOCO (primary, 12 conditions, 10+ generations) and Flickr30k (secondary, 5 conditions, 8 generations)—using Qwen2.5-VL-7B and FLUX.1-dev in iterative generate-retrain loops. Conditions include no verification, single-modal verification (×2), frozen cross-modal mutual verification, co-trained cross-modal verification, oracle upper bound, Gao & Li corpus injection, real+synthetic data mixing (50/50), data accumulation with real data, and three ρ-sensitivity settings. The dual-dataset evaluation tests generalizability across different image-text distributions (COCO's object-focused categories vs. Flickr30k's diverse everyday scenes). This work bridges multimodal co-evolutionary dynamics, verification theory, and pluralistic curation into a unified framework for sustainable multimodal synthetic data generation."

  "approach": "We formalize a verification-based stabilization protocol for co-evolving multimodal generative loops, directly addressing the Matthew effect and mutual amplification dynamics identified by Gao & Li (2503.08117).

**Frozen-Snapshot Cross-Modal Verification Protocol.** At each generation t, frozen snapshots of the VLM from generation t−1 and the diffusion model from generation t−1 serve as mutual cross-modal verifiers. The frozen VLM scores newly generated images via VQAScore for text-image alignment, while the frozen diffusion model's CLIP embedding similarity verifies caption fidelity. Only samples passing both verifiers (above learned thresholds τ_VLM and τ_diff calibrated on a held-out validation set) enter the next training set. This frozen-snapshot design resolves the circularity problem: verifiers do not co-degrade because they are fixed checkpoints from the previous generation, satisfying the external fixed-quality verifier assumption of Yi et al.'s ceiling theorem within each generation. This also directly extends the frozen relabeling strategy from the ICMI 2025 multimodal collapse paper into a principled verification framework.

**Verifier Quality Trajectory Across Generations.** A critical distinction: the frozen verifier is fixed within each generation t (satisfying the stationary verifier assumption of Theorem 4.1 in Yi et al. 2510.16657 for within-generation convergence), but the verifier quality evolves across generations since the snapshot from generation t−1 differs from that of t−2. We formalize this non-stationarity explicitly. Define D(g) = d(p_g, p_real) as the distributional distance between the generation-g model's output and the real data distribution. The effective verifier precision at generation g is α_eff(g) = h(D(g−1), ρ), a function of the previous generation's model quality and cross-modal correlation—better models yield more precise frozen verifiers. We derive a recursive contraction bound:
  D(g) ≤ γ(ρ, α_eff(g)) · D(g−1) + ε
where γ(ρ, α) < 1 for ρ < ρ* and sufficiently high verifier precision, and ε captures irreducible filtering noise.

**Strong convergence (conditional on Assumption 1).** Under the Uniform Improvement Regularity assumption (Assumption 1, defined below), α_eff(g) is non-decreasing, yielding a monotonically contracting sequence: D(0) ≥ D(1) ≥ D(2) ≥ ... → D* = ε/(1−γ*), where γ* = lim γ(ρ, α_eff(g)). The fixed point D* is strictly smaller than the single-verifier fixed point when ρ < ρ*, providing a formal guarantee that cross-modal verification yields strictly better long-run stability. The convergence rate is exponential: D(g) − D* ≤ (D(0) − D*) · γ_max^g.

**Assumption 1 (Uniform Improvement Regularity).** The cross-modal verification-induced improvement in distributional distance is uniform across modes: for any mode m with probability mass p_real(m) > δ (where δ is a negligible mass threshold), the local distributional distance satisfies D_m(g) ≤ D_m(g−1). Informally, this requires that improvement is not concentrated in dominant modes while rare modes degrade—a condition that cross-modal verification is specifically designed to promote by filtering samples from both modalities, providing diversifying pressure against the Matthew effect. We note that this assumption can be violated when models exhibit the 'self-improvement reversal' phenomenon (Wu et al. 2024), where aggregate benchmark improvement masks diversity loss and per-mode regression. Cross-modal verification mitigates but does not eliminate this risk; the assumption must therefore be validated empirically.

**Amortized convergence (unconditional).** Even without Assumption 1, we prove a weaker but unconditional convergence result. Define the amortized contraction rate Γ_G = (∏_{g=1}^{G} γ(ρ, α_eff(g)))^{1/G}—the geometric mean of per-generation contraction factors. If Γ_G < 1 for sufficiently large G (equivalently, if limsup_{G→∞} (1/G) Σ_{g=1}^{G} log γ(ρ, α_eff(g)) < 0), then D(g) → 0 almost surely, though convergence may be non-monotonic. This condition requires only that 'good generations' (where α_eff is high and γ < 1) dominate 'bad generations' in the geometric mean—a substantially weaker requirement than strict monotonicity. We empirically track both α_eff(g) and the running geometric mean Γ_g at each generation to determine which convergence regime applies.

In contrast, without verification (baseline condition 1), Gao & Li's analysis shows D(g) → ∞ (unbounded divergence). We validate the verifier quality trajectory empirically by tracking D(g) via FID and α_eff(g) via verifier precision/recall on held-out annotated samples at each generation.

**ρ-Parameterized Theoretical Framework.** We extend Yi et al.'s verifier ceiling theorem to a two-verifier multimodal setting without assuming perfect orthogonality. We model each modality's verification error as e_VLM = b_shared + b_visual and e_diff = b_shared + b_linguistic, where b_shared captures correlated bias (from shared pretraining data / joint vision-language features) and b_visual, b_linguistic capture modality-specific biases. The cross-modal bias correlation is defined directly as ρ = Corr(e_VLM, e_diff)—the Pearson correlation between the two verification error vectors. Under the symmetric case Var(b_visual) = Var(b_linguistic), this reduces to ρ = Var(b_shared)/(Var(b_shared) + Var(b_modality)), the proportion of variance due to shared bias. We derive convergence bounds as explicit functions of ρ:
  - At ρ=0 (perfect decorrelation): the two-verifier system achieves maximum improvement, with effective precision scaling as the sum of individual precisions.
  - At ρ=1 (fully correlated): degenerates to the single-verifier ceiling.
  - We prove existence of a critical threshold ρ* < 1 (depending on individual verifier precisions α_VLM, α_diff) below which cross-modal mutual verification provably surpasses the single-verifier ceiling.
We further show that the frozen cross-modal verification setup satisfies a ρ-relaxed version of Falahati et al.'s pluralistic curation conditions (specifically, the disjoint basins condition is relaxed to a ρ-dependent leakage bound), yielding collapse resistance guarantees that degrade gracefully with increasing ρ. For K>2 modalities (e.g., adding audio), we provide a theoretical corollary on how effective verifier precision scales with K under a structured correlation matrix, but this remains an unvalidated extension.

**Empirical Validation.** We validate on two datasets: (a) MSCOCO (~118K training images, 5 captions each) as the primary benchmark with the full 12-condition sweep, and (b) Flickr30k (~29K training images, 5 captions each) as a secondary generalizability benchmark with 5 core conditions. Flickr30k provides a complementary evaluation: its images are more diverse everyday scenes (vs. COCO's 80 object categories), captions are more descriptive and varied, and the smaller dataset size tests the framework under lower-data conditions where collapse pressure may be stronger.

**Primary evaluation (MSCOCO).** Iterative generate-retrain loops (10+ generations) using Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct as the VLM and FLUX.1-dev as the diffusion model. We measure FID, CIDEr, and VQAScore degradation curves across twelve conditions:
  (1) No verification—baseline reproducing Gao & Li's collapse dynamics and the Matthew effect.
  (2) Single-modal verification—VLM-only scoring.
  (3) Single-modal verification—diffusion-only scoring.
  (4) Cross-modal mutual verification with frozen snapshots—our primary method.
  (5) Cross-modal mutual verification with co-trained (non-frozen) verifiers—ablation testing the circularity concern; we predict this performs worse than frozen, validating the theoretical requirement.
  (6) Oracle verifier upper bound—filtering against ground-truth MSCOCO annotations.
  (7) Gao & Li's corpus injection strategy applied to the same experimental setup.
  (8) Real+synthetic data mixing (50/50)—at each generation, train on 50% real MSCOCO data + 50% newly generated synthetic data, following Bertrand et al. (ICLR 2024).
  (9) Data accumulation—train on the union of real MSCOCO data and all synthetic data from all previous generations, following Gerstgrasser et al. (COLM 2024).
  (10-12) Three ρ-sensitivity settings with artificially increased cross-modal correlation.

**Secondary evaluation (Flickr30k).** Five core conditions (1, 2, 3, 4, 8) over 8 generations using the same model architectures. This subset captures the key comparison: no verification vs. single-modal vs. cross-modal vs. data mixing, testing whether the relative ordering of methods holds on a different dataset with different image-text distribution characteristics. Per-generation cost is lower (~5.5 GPU-hrs) due to the smaller dataset.

**Empirical ρ Estimation Protocol.** We replace the previously proposed ad hoc mapping ρ̂ ≈ (ρ̂_S + 1)/2 with a principled derivation grounded in copula theory. The three complementary measures are:
  (a) **Spearman rank correlation (ρ̂_S) with Gaussian copula inversion:** Compute per-sample VQAScore (from VLM) and CLIP embedding similarity (from diffusion model) on the held-out validation set (5K for MSCOCO, 1K for Flickr30k) at each generation. The Spearman rank correlation ρ̂_S between these score vectors estimates rank-order dependence. Under the Gaussian copula model for the joint score distribution, the classical result (Kruskal 1958; see e.g. Nelsen 2006, Ch. 5) provides the exact relationship ρ_S = (6/π)·arcsin(ρ/2), which inverts to ρ = 2·sin(πρ̂_S/6). This mapping is exact when the joint distribution of verification scores follows a Gaussian copula, and remains a close approximation otherwise (the maximum deviation |ρ_S − ρ| ≤ 0.018 under the Gaussian copula). We test the Gaussian copula assumption via Cramér–von Mises goodness-of-fit tests on the empirical copula at each generation.
  (b) **Cohen's kappa (κ̂):** Binarize each verifier's scores at their respective thresholds (τ_VLM, τ_diff) and compute Cohen's κ on the accept/reject decisions. This provides a nonparametric measure of beyond-chance agreement on the actual filtering decisions, requiring no distributional assumptions. Low κ (κ < 0.4) indicates substantial disagreement, supporting the decorrelation hypothesis.
  (c) **Conditional disagreement rate:** The fraction of samples accepted by exactly one verifier but rejected by the other. This directly quantifies complementary information without any parametric assumptions.
  The three measures triangulate the decorrelation estimate: ρ̂_S with Gaussian copula inversion provides the quantitative mapping to the theoretical ρ under stated assumptions; κ̂ and the disagreement rate provide assumption-free qualitative validation. If the Gaussian copula assumption is rejected by the goodness-of-fit test, we report the Spearman correlation directly as a monotone proxy for ρ (since ρ_S is a monotonically increasing function of ρ for any copula, ordinal comparisons remain valid even without exact quantitative mapping). We track all three measures across generations on both datasets to verify that decorrelation is maintained as models co-evolve.

**ρ-Sensitivity Ablations.** (a) Artificially increase ρ by fine-tuning both models on shared intermediate representations (forcing error correlation) at three levels (moderate, high, near-unity), then observe degradation of collapse resistance to empirically locate the ρ* threshold and compare with theoretical predictions. (b) Compare empirical ρ̂ between Qwen2.5-VL (jointly trained vision-language) and a pipeline approach (separate vision encoder + LLM) to understand how joint vs. modular training affects cross-modal decorrelation.",
